opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it was pretty predictable, honestly. If you look at what a vector database actually does, the core piece, approximate nearest neighbor search over embeddings, is really an index. It's a feature, not a whole system. And historically, whenever a new kind of index comes along, whether it was full-text search, geospatial, or time series, there's a period where standalone systems pop up, and then the existing data platforms absorb that capability. Postgres got pgvector, the search engines added vector support, and the lakehouse and warehouse platforms added vector search too.

So the vector database companies were in a tricky position. If all you offer is the index, customers start asking, "Why do I need to copy my data into another system, keep it in sync, manage permissions twice, and pay for another service, just to get one kind of query?" In real applications you almost never do pure vector search. You want filtering on metadata, joins with your other tables, access control, freshness guarantees, keyword search alongside semantic search, and reranking. Once you add all of that, you're basically building a database, so moving toward general storage is the natural response.

The challenge is that general-purpose data management is a very hard and crowded space. Transactions, governance, scaling, backups, cost-efficient storage on object stores: the established systems have spent decades on that. So I think some of these companies will find good niches, especially where they've built a great developer experience or really optimized serving at scale. But for most enterprises, the gravity is toward keeping the data where it already lives and bringing the vector capability to it, rather than the other way around.

The broader lesson, which I think applies to a lot of the AI infrastructure wave, is that the hard part of these applications usually isn't any single component. It's the system around it: getting the right data, keeping it governed and fresh, and evaluating the quality of what comes out. The winners will be the ones who make that whole pipeline easier, not just one step of it.

r001.rationale: The response calls the move into general storage a natural response and compares vector search with earlier specialized database features. But its broader historical pattern is that established platforms absorb new capabilities, not that companies expand beyond their initial specialized offering.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually a pretty natural evolution, and honestly it's one we saw coming from the data infrastructure side. In 2023 there was this huge wave of interest in vector search because of RAG, and a bunch of companies built very good specialized systems for one operation: approximate nearest neighbor search over embeddings. That's a real, hard engineering problem. But once you actually try to build an application on it, you realize that the vector is almost never the whole story. You need the original text, you need metadata, you need filters, you need access controls, you need to join against the rest of your enterprise data, you need to update things when the source documents change. So very quickly these systems get pulled toward being a general storage and query engine, because that's what the application actually requires.

And the flip side is happening too. If you look at Postgres with pgvector, or what Databricks and others are doing in the lakehouse, or even Elasticsearch, all the existing data systems are adding vector indexes as just another index type. From their point of view, a vector index is not that different from a B-tree or a full-text index. It's one more way to access the data you already govern and manage. So you've got the specialized players moving toward general storage, and the general storage players absorbing the specialized capability, and they meet somewhere in the middle.

My personal view is that the general systems have a structural advantage here, because the hard part for most organizations isn't the index, it's everything around the data: lineage, permissions, freshness, cost. Those are problems people have already solved once for their analytical data, and they don't want to solve them a second time in a separate silo just because the access pattern is now a similarity search. There's a long history of this in databases. Object databases, XML databases, graph databases, time series databases: every few years a new data type shows up, specialized engines emerge, and then the mainstream systems absorb the useful ideas. Some of the specialized companies survive by going deep on a particular workload, like very high-QPS, very low-latency serving. But the broad market tends to consolidate around systems that treat the new thing as a feature rather than a product.

The one caveat I'd add is that the AI workload is changing fast enough that it's not obvious yet what the right abstraction is. Maybe it's vectors, maybe it's something more like an agent with tools over structured and unstructured data, maybe the embedding model and the index get co-designed in a way that's hard to retrofit. So I don't think it's over. But the move toward general storage is these companies correctly recognizing that a standalone vector index is a thin wedge, and they need to own more of the stack to stay relevant.

r001.rationale: The response describes vector database companies moving from specialized vector search toward general storage, then places that shift within a recurring database pattern in which specialized systems emerge and mainstream systems absorb their useful capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think it reflects the fact that vector search is a capability you want in a database, but it’s not necessarily a separate database category. If you’re building an application, you usually need more than the nearest vectors. You need to filter by metadata, check permissions, update records, and combine the results with other data.

So there are two directions you can come at this from. Existing databases can add vector search, and vector databases can add more general database functionality. Both end up moving toward a system that handles more of the application’s needs. The question is whether specializing in vector search gives you enough of an advantage to justify having another system in your stack.

r001.rationale: The response says vector databases are adding general functionality and existing databases are adding vector search, but it does not frame this as part of a broader pattern of companies expanding beyond their initial specialized offerings.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it reflects the fact that vector search is usually one part of an application, rather than the whole application. You have embeddings, but you also have the original documents, metadata, permissions, and other data you want to filter or join against. If those live in separate systems, you have to keep everything synchronized, and that gets complicated pretty quickly.

So there are two directions you can come at this from. You can start with a vector database and add more general storage and query capabilities, or you can start with a general-purpose database and add vector search. Both are trying to give developers fewer systems to manage. The interesting question is where a specialized system gives you enough of an advantage to justify that extra complexity.

r001.rationale: The response describes vector databases adding general storage and general databases adding vector search, but it does not frame this as a broader pattern of companies expanding beyond their initial specialized offerings.
